title: Consensus and leader election: how machines agree when some of them fail
dek: Who is the leader? Did that write happen? Which settings are current? When several machines must give one answer, and any of them can pause, crash or lose the network, "just ask everyone" stops working. Majorities and numbered terms are how real systems get one answer anyway.

items: Some decisions must have exactly one answer across machines: who leads, whether a write was accepted, which job runner owns tonight's job. Machines can't tell a dead peer from a slow one, so they need a rule.
The rule is a majority. With 5 machines, a decision needs 3. Any two groups of 3 share at least one machine, so two different answers can never both win.
A leader is chosen by vote for a numbered term. Each machine votes once per term; a majority makes a leader; a machine that sees a higher term steps down.
An old leader can wake from a pause still thinking it leads. Stop it by putting the term number on every write and rejecting writes from older terms.
Don't write this yourself. Use etcd, ZooKeeper or Consul, or a database that has it built in, and know what it costs: every decision waits for a majority, and a side without one stops.

body.x: Zotato runs the 9 pm payout job, which pays every restaurant for the day, on one of three machines. It must run exactly once. The obvious plan is "machine 1 runs it; if machine 1 is down, machine 2 does". But machine 2 can't see whether machine 1 is down. It can only see that machine 1 hasn't answered for a while, and that also happens when machine 1 is busy, paused for garbage collection, or cut off by the network while still running the job.

items: There's no shared clock: each machine's clock drifts, and a paused process doesn't notice time passing.
Messages arrive late, out of order, or not at all, and there's no way to tell "lost" from "slow".
The network can split machines into groups that each think the others are dead.

body.cap: Five machines, three in Mumbai and two in Hyderabad. The link breaks. The three are a majority and keep going; the two aren't, so they refuse writes and wait. The two sides can never both decide.

body.x: A committee of five where any decision needs three signatures. If two members are stuck in traffic, the other three can still sign. Two members on their own can't, however sure they are.

A majority (a quorum) is more than half. The trick is that any two majorities of the same group overlap in at least one machine, and that machine has saved to disk what it already agreed to. So if one majority decided "A leads term 5", no other majority can decide "C leads term 5".

That's why groups are odd: 4 machines survive no more failures than 3, and every decision has to wait for one more answer. Most systems use 3 or 5. Spread them over places that fail separately, such as three zones of a region, or two cities plus a third as a tiebreaker.

items: The leader sends a small heartbeat to the others every few dozen milliseconds.
Each follower waits a random time, say 150 to 300 ms. If no heartbeat arrives in that time, it starts a new term: term number + 1, a vote for itself, and a request for votes to everyone.
Each machine votes for at most one candidate per term, and only for one whose record of decisions is at least as complete as its own.
A candidate with votes from a majority becomes leader for that term and starts sending heartbeats.
The random wait matters: one follower usually wakes first and wins before anyone else asks. If two ask at once and split the vote, both wait a new random time and try again.

body.cap: A leads term 4 and stops. B's random wait runs out first, so it starts term 5 and asks for votes. C hasn't voted in term 5 and says yes: two of three is a majority. If A comes back, it sees term 5 and steps down.

body.x: The leader that doesn't know it was replaced

Machine 1 starts the payout job, then pauses for 20 seconds. The others elect machine 2, which starts the job too. Machine 1 wakes up mid-job, still sure it leads. For a moment, two machines are paying restaurants.

body.name: First try
body.what: The leader holds a lease for 10 seconds and renews it; others wait for it to expire before taking over.
body.use: Easy, and fine when an extra run does no harm.
body.avoid: A paused process doesn't know its lease ran out. It wakes up and acts before it checks the clock.
body.ex: Machine 1 pauses with 3 seconds of lease left, wakes 20 seconds later, and sends one more batch of payouts.
body.like: A guest who dozed off in a hotel room and walks out past checkout still holding the key.

body.name: Better
body.what: Every action carries the leader's term number. Whatever it writes to (the payouts table, storage) remembers the highest term it has seen and rejects anything older.
body.use: The old leader can wake up and try whatever it likes: its writes say term 4, the store has seen term 5, and they're refused.
body.avoid: Everything the leader writes to must check the number. A bank's API won't, so send each payout with a unique id the bank uses to ignore repeats.
body.ex: Machine 1 sends "pay batch 7, term 4". The payouts table has seen term 5 and refuses it.
body.like: A new guard changes the lock code; the old guard's code no longer opens the door, however confident he is.

items: Every decision waits for a majority to answer. Inside one region that's a millisecond or two. With machines in Mumbai and Hyderabad, every write waits for a round trip between cities.

All writes go through the leader, so it's the limit on how many decisions a second the group can make. That's why you use consensus for small, important things (who leads, which settings are current), not for every order.
While a new leader is being chosen, a few hundred milliseconds to a few seconds, nothing new is decided.
A side without a majority stops accepting writes. It's choosing to be right over being available, the C in CAP.

etcd, ZooKeeper and Consul run consensus for you. Typical uses: pick a leader (whoever holds a key leads, and the key comes with a fencing number), store settings that must be the same everywhere, keep a list of which services are up.
Many databases replicate with consensus inside (Raft is a common choice), so you get a safe failover without running it yourself.
Writing your own is a classic way to lose data in rare cases that no test finds. Interviewers like hearing that you'd use a proven one.
When a design has "one leader" or "run this exactly once", say how the leader is chosen and what stops two at once.
Use majorities with numbers: 3 machines survive 1 failure, 5 survive 2.
Mention fencing (the term number on every write) whenever an old leader could act after a pause.
Say what happens during a split: the side without a majority stops writing, and why that's the right choice for payments.

body.x: In the Lab's cache-restart challenge, the cache crashes in the middle of dinner. Watch which parts of your design keep going and which ones struggle, the same question consensus answers for leaders.
